newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee jumps to 17-mth highs, upswing resumes.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee jumps to 17-mth highs, upswing resumes.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures surged to 17-month highs in roller coaster dealings Thursday, as speculators bought heavily amid bullish technical indicators and persistent supply concerns, traders said.
"This market is behaving well technically and it's supported by the fundamentals," said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast.
"The outlook is for tighter supply because there is the potential for Brazil's crop to be sizably lower," she said, "and the presumption of residual delays in Colombia after the dockworkers' strike."
March delivery shot up to a fresh life-of-contract high of 151.50 cents per lb before closing at 150.80 cents, up 6.25 cents on the day. Early in the session, March sunk to a low of 142.60 cents.
Second-month May finished 5.60 cents higher, to 144.80 cents, while the back months rose 3.50 to 4.90 cents.

Prices headed lower at the opening Thursday, as the market followed through on profit-taking seen yesterday. But rumors that Procter & Gamble Co's Folgers Coffee would raise their retail coffee prices prompted some trade buying and turned the market around.
"The market was jogged by the rumor Folgers was going to raise its price," Prendergast said.
A spokeswoman at the company vehemently denied these rumors, but traders said the market's momentum had shifted anyway.

Technically, traders said today's key reversal -- making lower lows than the previous session while ending above its high -- was positive for the market. They said March's fresh high of 151.50 would provide initial resistance, with a strong upside target seen at 155.00.

Fundamentally, supply jitters were heightened by news a debtors' strike declared Wednesday by Colombia's independent coffee growers could support an overall trend toward lower output from the world's second-biggest coffee producer.

Industry sources in Colombia warned if members of the country's leading independent coffee growers' association made good on their promise to withhold payments on all past-due loans, banks may have no choice but to foreclose on mortgages and seize control of about 50,000 plantations.
That, in turn, could lead to the abandonment of a large number of coffee farms, they said.
Volume Wednesday was heavy, at an estimated 15,270 lots.
